clue.text: Ambush European soldier heading north, such as Cyrano de Bergerac

indicators.note: in a down entry, heading north means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a private soldier is one of the men

explanation.surface: A soldier from Europe heads north to ambush the famous swordsman Cyrano de Bergerac.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyrano is a first name and de Bergerac a surname, so each is a NAME PART.
explanation.definitionFit: Each element of Cyrano's full name, the forename or the family title, is one component of his complete name.

clue.text: Intelligence shown by bidders giving their opponents hiding

indicators.note: the partnership is hiding the opposing pair, keeping them tucked inside

parts.note: in bridge, North and South bid as partners
East and West are the opposing bridge partnership

explanation.surface: At an auction, how some bidders behave reveals information while they conceal their rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge players are named by compass points: North-South play against East-West.
explanation.definitionFit: Intelligence in the sense of information or tidings received is a synonym for reports of recent events.

clue.text: Gain nothing in this quarter? Be selective

indicators.note: one thing placed in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: the north-west is one quarter of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone told they gain nothing in this area is advised to be choosier.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle has a compass theme, so 'this quarter' is a compass quarter rather than a district or a fraction.
explanation.definitionFit: To winnow is literally to separate grain from chaff, and figuratively to sift out the best and discard the rest.

clue.text: Mineral's in there, mixed with phosphorus

indicators.note: things that are mixed are jumbled up into a different order

parts.note: P is the chemical symbol for phosphorus

explanation.surface: A geologist notes that a mineral sample contains phosphorus mixed through it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nephrite is a hard green mineral, one of the two stones known as jade.

clue.text: Negative response about flowers in strong winds

parts.note: re means concerning, as in letters

explanation.surface: Someone says no when asked about flowers being battered in a gale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowers' could be rivers in cryptic code, but here they are simply garden blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: A nor'easter is a powerful gale blowing from the north-east, especially on the US Atlantic coast.

clue.text: Enters the exam, exhausted, to get prize

indicators.note: exhausted words are emptied out, so only their outermost letters remain

explanation.surface: A student sits a gruelling exam, worn out, in order to win an award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prize' is a verb here, meaning to value highly, not the award the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To prize something is to value it greatly, which is to hold it in high regard.

clue.text: Hesitant, using gestural and verbal forms of communication

parts.note: a wave is a gesture of the hand
a ring is a phone call, spoken contact

explanation.surface: Someone unsure of themselves resorts to both gestures and words to get a message across.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forms of communication' serves both adjectives: a gestural form and a verbal one.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone wavering is undecided, faltering between options, which is what being hesitant describes.

clue.text: Three quarters of strategy rearranged in turn

indicators.note: rearranged letters are put into a new order
taking three quarters of an eight-letter word means dropping a quarter, two letters

parts.note: taken as written; the first quarter is dropped

explanation.surface: Most of a plan is reorganised in its turn.
explanation.definitionFit: To gyrate is to spin or revolve, which is what turning around a centre means.

clue.text: Name of girl I see misrepresented in contents of blog? Just the opposite

indicators.note: this reverses the stated 'in', so the second part goes inside the first instead
something misrepresented is distorted, so its letters are muddled
the contents of a word are its inner letters, without the ends

explanation.surface: A girl's name is spotted written wrongly in the text of an online post.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the scrambled I SEE goes inside LO; 'Just the opposite' flips that, putting LO inside the scramble.
explanation.definitionFit: Eloise is a female given name, the French form famous from Abelard and Heloise.

clue.text: Point, or points, one repeated

parts.note: three compass points: north, east, south
the last of those points used a second time

explanation.surface: A debater makes a point, or several, with one of them repeated.
explanation.walkthrough: A ness is a headland, a point of land jutting into the sea, as in Sheerness or Dungeness.
explanation.definitionFit: A ness is a promontory or headland, a geographical point of land projecting into water.

clue.text: The money ran out, eliminating a former Middle East country

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or askew, so the letters are thrown into disorder
eliminating something removes it from the collection of letters

explanation.surface: A state's cash ran dry, wiping out a nation that once existed in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The money ran out' reads as a story of bankruptcy; the A of RAN is dropped before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: North Yemen was a separate state until it merged with South Yemen in 1990, so it no longer exists.

clue.text: Used to lack experience, but following advice to young man? Capital!

indicators.note: the famous advice is 'Go west, young man', and going west means reading leftwards

parts.note: as in 'used to be', past tense of be

explanation.surface: An older man who was once inexperienced took advice to young men, a capital idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go west, young man' is a famous American saying; in an across entry west is leftwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Warsaw is the capital city of Poland, so it is an example of a capital.

clue.text: Opposite of 5 hats

indicators.note: taking the opposite means swapping each compass direction for its counterpart

explanation.surface: Headwear named as the reverse of the strong winds in another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap north for south and east for west in NOR'EASTERS to get SOU'WESTERS.
explanation.definitionFit: A sou'wester is a waterproof oilskin hat with a broad brim at the back, worn by sailors.

clue.text: Heavy work, including some art, is laborious

indicators.note: a thing including another holds it inside itself

parts.note: a tome is a heavy, weighty book
oil paintings are one kind of art

explanation.surface: Hard labour, even with a bit of painting thrown in, remains tiresome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavy work' suggests toil, but it is a weighty book.
explanation.definitionFit: Toilsome describes something requiring hard, wearying effort, the same as a laborious task.

clue.text: Shown how tense it can be in hearing

indicators.note: in hearing means as it sounds when spoken, not as spelt

explanation.surface: Someone is demonstrating how nervous a person can get when attending a hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Taught is the past participle of teach, and being taught something means being shown how to do it.

clue.text: Intellectual heard greeting bishop on street

indicators.note: heard means the word as spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
a row is a street of houses, as in Savile Row

explanation.surface: A clever thinker is overheard saying hello to a bishop out in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A highbrow is a person of refined, scholarly tastes, an intellectual noun or adjective.

clue.text: Get worked on, using pliers and saw

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: what pliers do to an object
second meaning: observed, past tense of see

explanation.surface: Instructions in a workshop about tackling a job with pliers and a saw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a tool alongside pliers, but it is the past tense of see. Split, the answer reads BE HELD, what pliers do.
explanation.definitionFit: Beheld is the past tense of behold, an old-fashioned way of saying looked at or observed.

clue.text: Dislike neighbourhood being restricted, with east in disarray

indicators.note: a restricted word is cut short, here to its standard abbreviation

parts.note: a district is a neighbourhood or area

indicators.note: things in disarray are out of order and need reordering

explanation.surface: Residents resent their area being hemmed in while its eastern side is in chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: DIST is the usual shortened form of district.
explanation.definitionFit: Distaste is a feeling of aversion or mild disgust, which a noun for dislike also expresses.

clue.text: Appropriate, as birds turning up from the south

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up from the bottom means the letters run backwards

parts.note: emus are large flightless Australian birds

explanation.surface: Flocks of birds appear, coming up from the south, as is fitting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' is a verb here, meaning to take over, not the adjective meaning suitable.
explanation.definitionFit: To assume power or control is to seize or take it for oneself, which is what appropriate means as a verb.

clue.text: Fuel was spread over grate, haphazardly

indicators.note: something done haphazardly is done at random, without any order

explanation.surface: Coal or wood for a fire was scattered carelessly across the fireplace.
explanation.definitionFit: Water gas is a fuel gas made by passing steam over red-hot coke, giving hydrogen and carbon monoxide.

clue.text: Treasures commercial products of mine

parts.note: ores are the minerals dug from a mine

explanation.surface: Valuables advertised as goods dug from a mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Treasures' is a verb, and 'commercial' a noun meaning an advert.
explanation.definitionFit: To treasure someone is to cherish and love them deeply, which is what the verb adores conveys.

clue.text: Exploit source of inspiration when lives lost

indicators.note: something lost in another thing is buried inside it

parts.note: to live is to be, so lives gives is

explanation.surface: Taking advantage of someone's inspiration even when lives are lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost' suggests removing letters, but here the lives are lost inside the muse.
explanation.definitionFit: To exploit someone or something is to use it wrongly for your own ends, which misuse also means.

clue.text: Crazy artists recalled city in Asia

explanation.surface: A group of wild painters reminisce about a city in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' looks like a reversal signal, but belongs with the definition: the city is now called Chennai, so Madras is its former name.
explanation.definitionFit: Madras is the former name of Chennai, the large city in south-east India, renamed in 1996.

clue.text: Keep quiet about escape before spring, heading for sunshine?

indicators.note: about means going round, so the first piece surrounds the next

parts.note: a way out is an escape
to spring is to leap or bound

explanation.surface: A prisoner keeps quiet about an escape planned for spring, then heads off to the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season of the escape, but it is a leap.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelling southbound means going south, which in the northern hemisphere usually means towards warmer, sunnier places.

clue.text: Leaves from Asia — temperature in that part of world has shifted

indicators.note: a letter that has shifted has moved from one end of the word to the other

explanation.surface: Tea leaves come from Asia, where the climate has been changing.
explanation.walkthrough: The T in EAST stands for temperature; it moves from the end to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Teas are the dried leaves of the tea plant, much of it grown in India, China and Sri Lanka.

clue.text: Middle East abandoned by major power? So it is

indicators.note: something abandoned is left behind and removed from the word

parts.note: E for East, here sitting in the middle

explanation.surface: A superpower withdraws from the Middle East, and that is how things stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle East' is not the region: it is an E in the middle of THE US.
explanation.definitionFit: Thus and so are both adverbs meaning therefore, or in this manner.

clue.text: Odd character that is moved around in anagram of word

indicators.note: moved around means turned about, so the short phrase is read backwards
one thing in another means it sits inside it
this says outright that the following letters are rearranged

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is

explanation.surface: A self-referential note on how a strange character gets shuffled within a word puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue jokes that it is describing itself, with 'anagram' used openly.
explanation.definitionFit: A weirdo is an informal word for an eccentric or strange person, an odd character.

clue.text: Clear area in emergency, initially — very critical

indicators.note: one thing in another means it sits inside it
initially means taking just the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Instructions to clear a zone during a crisis that has become very serious.
explanation.definitionFit: To evacuate a building or area is to empty it of people, clearing it.
